summary: Defines an IMAP extension, Conditional STORE, that helps multiple clients coordinate changes to a shared mailbox. It lets clients quickly resynchronize flag changes and ensures that one client does not overwrite another's changes. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 7162.

eli5.summary: Two people edit the same shopping list. This feature lets each see if the other changed something before saving, so nobody's changes are lost.

questions: how to sync flags in imap
subtitle: Conditional flag updates and quick resynchronization for shared IMAP mailboxes.

tldr.problem: When multiple IMAP clients access the same mailbox, they need to coordinate flag changes (like marking messages as read or deleted) without one client overwriting another's changes. Clients also need to quickly detect what has changed since they last synchronized.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds modification sequences (mod-sequences), which are opaque 64-bit values that increase each time any message metadata changes. Clients can use UNCHANGEDSINCE in STORE commands to update flags only if the message hasn't changed since they last checked, and use CHANGEDSINCE in FETCH to quickly find messages that changed.
tldr.outcome: Multiple clients can now safely share mailboxes without losing updates, and can resynchronize efficiently without downloading entire flag lists. This was later updated by RFC 7162.

today: RFC 4551 is a Standards Track specification that is widely implemented in IMAP servers and clients. It was later updated and refined by RFC 7162, which provides additional guidance and clarifications. The modification sequence mechanism is now essential for reliable multi-client mailbox synchronization.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) allows clients to manage mailboxes on a server. The base protocol works well for a single client, but problems arise when multiple clients need to coordinate changes to the same mailbox. Examples include different clients for the same user, multiple users accessing a shared mailbox, or an application using an IMAP mailbox as a message queue with multiple dequeueing clients.

The core problem is state synchronization: how can a client know if another client has modified message flags (metadata) since it last checked? The Conditional STORE facility provides a protected update mechanism that can detect and resolve conflicts between multiple writing clients, and allows clients to quickly resynchronize after a disconnection by identifying only the messages that have actually changed.
sections.eli5: IMAP mailboxes are like shared documents in the cloud. When multiple people have it open, they need a way to see what changed and make sure nobody accidentally overwrites someone else's work.

sections.title: Modification Sequences
sections.content:
The RFC requires IMAP servers to associate a modification sequence (mod-sequence) with every message. A mod-sequence is a positive unsigned 64-bit value that the server updates whenever any message metadata item is modified. The server MUST guarantee that each STORE command on the same mailbox gets a different mod-sequence value, and that for any two successive STORE operations on the same mailbox, the second one has a greater mod-sequence than the first.

When a message is appended to a mailbox or when existing metadata changes, the server updates the message's mod-sequence to a value higher than any previous mod-sequence in the mailbox. Notably, the RFC disallows using system clock as mod-sequence because clock adjustments (e.g., NTP corrections) could cause the value to decrease, violating the monotonicity requirement.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a version number. Every time someone changes the message's flags or other data, the version number goes up. Version numbers always go up—never down.

sections.title: Conditional STORE and UNCHANGED SINCE
sections.content:
The RFC adds an UNCHANGEDSINCE modifier to the STORE command. When a client issues STORE with UNCHANGEDSINCE, the server performs the requested flag change only if the message's mod-sequence is less than or equal to the value specified. If the message's mod-sequence is greater (meaning another client modified it), the operation is not performed.

Even if the .SILENT suffix is used, the server MUST send an untagged FETCH response containing the current MODSEQ value of the message. The server also tracks which messages failed the UNCHANGEDSINCE test and returns a MODIFIED response code listing them. This allows the client to learn which messages were not updated and retry with the correct current mod-sequence.
sections.eli5: You say 'mark this message as read, but only if its version number hasn't changed since I last saw version 100'. If someone else already bumped it to version 101, the server says no and tells you the new version.

sections.title: Quick Resynchronization with FETCH and SEARCH
sections.content:
For fast resynchronization, the RFC adds CHANGEDSINCE to FETCH and MODSEQ to SEARCH. A client can issue FETCH with CHANGEDSINCE and a mod-sequence value to retrieve only messages that have been modified since that mod-sequence value. The server returns those messages along with their current mod-sequence values.

Alternatively, a client can use SEARCH MODSEQ to find all messages with a modification sequence at or above a given value. When combined with STATUS HIGHESTMODSEQ (which returns the highest mod-sequence of all messages in a mailbox), a client can quickly determine after a disconnection whether the mailbox has changed and download only the messages that actually changed, rather than re-fetching the entire mailbox.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking 'what are all the flags?', the client asks 'what messages changed since version 500?'. The server only sends back the ones that did.

sections.title: Server Behavior and Mailbox Support
sections.content:
Not all mailboxes need to support persistent mod-sequences. When a client selects a mailbox, the server returns either HIGHESTMODSEQ (if the mailbox supports persistent mod-sequences) or NOMODSEQ (if it does not). If a mailbox does not support mod-sequences, the server MUST reject any FETCH CHANGEDSINCE, SEARCH MODSEQ, or STORE UNCHANGEDSINCE command with a BAD response.

The RFC also specifies that servers implementing CONDSTORE should avoid spurious MODIFIED responses for +FLAGS or -FLAGS operations even when they store a single mod-sequence value per message, rather than separate mod-sequences for each metadata item. This optimization reduces unnecessary client retries when only unrelated metadata has changed.
sections.eli5: The server tells the client upfront: 'I track version numbers for this mailbox' or 'I don't'. If the client tries to use version numbers on a mailbox that doesn't support them, the server says 'not allowed'.

sections.title: Later Updates and RFC 7162
sections.content:
RFC 4551 was published in June 2006 as a Standards Track specification that updated RFC 3501 (IMAP4rev1). The CONDSTORE extension has been widely implemented and adopted by major IMAP servers and clients. In 2014, RFC 7162 provided an updated version with clarifications and additional guidance for client and server implementers.

RFC 4551 defines the core mechanism that has become essential for reliable multi-client mailbox access, but RFC 7162 is now the preferred reference for new implementations. However, RFC 4551 remains a valid and widely deployed specification that introduced the fundamental concepts of modification sequences and conditional updates to IMAP.
sections.eli5: This RFC solved a real problem that developers faced when they wanted to let multiple devices access the same email inbox safely. A newer RFC improved on it, but the original idea is still correct and still used.
